Finish with the approval block recording D-01, then work through Done when and Check yourself.
build.modelAnswer: A good charter fits on two pages. Every objective has a baseline, a target and a date. The milestones match the schedule, and the budget lines add to CAD 1,200,000 with the reserve shown separately. Each risk has an owner. Privacy and security success criteria name their evidence. The approval block records D-01: Dr. Helen Marchetti, 2026-09-01.

examTips.tip: Business Environment task 1 Define and establish project governance: the sponsor issues the charter and it gives the project manager authority. If a scenario has a PM without authority or a contested decision, the answer usually points back to the charter and the agreed governance.

Process task 1 Develop an integrated project management plan and plan delivery: the charter is high level. Detailed scope, schedule and cost baselines come after it, and once approved, changes to them go through integrated change control.

Security and Risk Management, 1.3 security governance principles: senior management is accountable for security and risk. Choose answers where leaders approve and own risk, and security professionals advise, rather than technicians accepting risk themselves.

Governance is one of the five ITIL Value System components (with guiding principles, value chain activities, management practices and continual improvement). Expect a question that asks which component directs and controls the organization.

pitfalls: Letting the Programme Manager approve the charter. The sponsor authorizes it; you draft it and run the work it authorizes.
Writing objectives that cannot be checked. Improve flow is not an objective; 80.5 to 60 minutes at KGH by a date is.
Leaving privacy and security out of success criteria. A release that meets its dates but skips the privacy impact assessment is not a success.
Editing the charter after approval. Changes to objectives, gates or budget go through the change-control board with a decision record.

check.q: Who issues the Beacon charter, and why is it not the Programme Manager?
check.a: Dr. Helen Marchetti, the executive sponsor, issues and approves it (D-01, 2026-09-01). The charter commits Kestrel's money and people and gives the Programme Manager authority, so it must come from someone with that authority. The Programme Manager usually drafts it.

check.q: Two weeks after approval, Release 1 looks likely to miss 2026-10-23 by three days. Can you update the gate date in the charter?
check.a: Not on your own. A change that moves a release gate goes to the change-control board chaired by Marcus Bell with an impact assessment, and the sponsor is informed. If approved, the decision is recorded and the baseline and charter reference updated.

check.q: Why does the charter make the privacy impact assessment a success criterion?
check.a: Because Release 1 uses health information, and section 64 of the Health Information Act requires a custodian to submit a privacy impact assessment to the Commissioner for review and comment before implementing a practice or system involving individually identifying health information. Making it a success criterion means go-live cannot be declared without it.

items.summary: You learn how to elicit real needs from emergency and patient-flow leaders: who to involve, which techniques to use, how to ask, and how to write requirements that can be tested. You open the requirements and traceability register with Release 1's needs and KPI definitions.

read.heading: Elicitation is not order-taking
read.body:
Elicitation draws out what people need, not only what they ask for. Leaders often ask for a solution: send me the extract earlier. Your job is to find the decision behind it: by the morning huddle I need to know which site is falling behind so I can move staff. Requirements describe needs and the conditions a solution must meet; design comes later.

In the Beacon schedule, task 3 Confirm requirements and KPI (key performance indicator) definitions has six working days (2026-09-01 to 2026-09-08) and zero float. It is on the critical path, so slow elicitation delays the Release 1 gate. Plan it tightly.

| Who | Why they matter |
|---|---|
| Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007), Emergency Medical Director | Owns emergency department (ED) data; confirms which waits matter and how they are defined |
| Janelle Cardinal (E-008), Director of Patient Flow | Main dashboard user; bed pressure and alternate level of care (ALC) |
| Aisha Mahmoud (E-010), ED Charge Nurse, KGH | What a shift lead needs at a glance |
| Dr. Liam O'Connor (E-012), ED Physician, ARH | Whether a community site sees the same picture |
| Ben Kowalski (E-011), Unit Clerk, KGH Medicine 4A | How bed status is entered |
| Mei Tanaka (E-013), Clinical Analyst | How today's extracts are built |
| Priya Raman (E-003), Chief Privacy Officer | What the data may contain |
| Grace Liu (E-005), Service Desk Manager | How the service will be supported |

read.heading: Choosing elicitation techniques
read.body:
No single technique is enough. Match the technique to what you need to learn.

| Technique | Best for | Beacon use |
|---|---|---|
| Interview | Depth, sensitive topics, senior people | One-to-one with Dr. Whitford and Janelle Cardinal |
| Facilitated workshop | Agreeing shared definitions across groups | KPI definitions with all four sites in one room |
| Observation (job shadowing) | Work people do without thinking about it | The KGH morning bed huddle; a charge nurse at the tracking board |
| Document analysis | The current state and existing rules | The emailed extracts, the data dictionary, the Canadian Triage and Acuity Scale (CTAS) guidelines |
| Questionnaire | Many people, simple questions | Frontline nurses at four sites on what they check each shift |
| Prototype | People who react better to something they can see | A paper sketch of the ED page to test before building |

Observation matters most where people describe the process they think they follow. A charge nurse may say she checks waits hourly, while watching shows she checks the tracking board every few minutes and needs the dashboard only for the morning picture. Document analysis matters because the disagreement between sites often hides in formulas inside the old extracts, where one site counts from triage and another from arrival.

read.heading: Asking questions that reveal needs
read.body:
Start open, then narrow. Open questions (What happens at the 08:00 huddle?) uncover needs; closed questions (Do you need it by site?) confirm details. When an answer is vague, ask why again until you reach the decision or the risk behind it.

A short interview guide for Janelle Cardinal:
1. Walk me through your morning. When do you first look at patient-flow numbers?
2. What decision do you make with them, and who acts on it?
3. Which number do you trust least today, and why?
4. When numbers from two sites disagree, what do you do?
5. What would you stop doing if the dashboard worked?
6. Who else should see this, and who should not?

Question 3 surfaces the trust problem. Question 6 surfaces privacy and access needs early, so they become requirements rather than late surprises.

Conflicting definitions are the most common finding. If KGH measures waits from triage and ARH from arrival, both are right by their own rule and the numbers will never agree. Elicitation ends with one agreed definition, signed off by the data owner. Kestrel's is: the ED clock starts at arrival (registration), time to physician initial assessment (PIA) is PIA minus arrival, ED length of stay is departure minus arrival, and left without being seen (LWBS) means the patient left before a PIA.

read.heading: Kinds of requirements
read.body:
Sort what you hear into types, because each is tested differently.

| Type | Answers | Beacon example |
|---|---|---|
| Business | Why the organization wants this | Reduce the LWBS rate across sites from 5.7% toward the agreed 4.5% |
| Stakeholder | What a group needs | Patient-flow leaders need one agreed view of ED waits and bed occupancy each morning |
| Functional | What the solution does | The ED page shows median minutes to PIA by site, CTAS level and month |
| Non-functional | How well it does it | Site users see only their own site's rows; pages meet accessibility checks |
| Transition | What is needed to move to the new way | Service desk knowledge articles; retiring the emailed extracts |

Constraints are also captured: the Health Information Act duties of least amount and highest anonymity, Kestrel's rule to suppress counts under 5 outside the care team, and the fixed go-live gate.

Give each requirement an ID, a source (the person or document it came from), a priority and a pass or fail acceptance criterion. Knowing its type tells you how to test it. The source is what makes traceability possible tomorrow.

read.heading: Writing requirements that can be tested
read.body:
A good requirement states one need, is clear to every reader, can be tested, is feasible and traces to a source. Words such as fast, user-friendly or real-time fail the test because nobody can prove them.

| Weak | Testable |
|---|---|
| The dashboard should be fast | Every visual on the ED page renders in 3 seconds or less in Performance Analyzer (agreed target) |
| Show waits | Show median minutes from arrival to PIA by site and CTAS level, using Kestrel's definition |
| Keep it secure | A user in the ARH role sees only ARH rows; a negative test shows KGH rows are hidden |
| Easy to use | A charge nurse finds today's LWBS count for her site in under three clicks during user acceptance testing |

Prioritize with MoSCoW: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time. Must items define the minimum release. A request that breaks a legal duty, such as names on a patient-flow dashboard, is not a priority question: it is out, with the reason recorded.

read.heading: The ITIL view: Discover and co-create
read.body:
In the ITIL Version 5 lifecycle, this work belongs to Discover: understanding consumers, their outcomes and the demand before you design. Four guiding principles shape it:
- Focus on value: ask what outcome each request serves for patients, clinicians and the organization.
- Start where you are: study the current extracts, definitions and workarounds before replacing them. Some parts, such as the CTAS reference and the site codes, can be reused.
- Collaborate and promote visibility: bring the four sites into one workshop and show the draft definitions to everyone, so disagreement surfaces early.
- Progress iteratively with feedback: test a sketch with Aisha Mahmoud before building pages.

Value is co-created. The analytics team cannot decide alone what useful means; the leaders who act on the numbers help define it, and they share responsibility for using the service well. That is why their sign-off on definitions is a requirement in itself.

keyTerms.definition: Drawing out stakeholders' real needs through interviews, workshops, observation, document analysis, questionnaires and prototypes, rather than recording requests as given.
What the solution must do, such as showing median minutes to PIA by site and CTAS level.
How well the solution must perform: security, accessibility, performance, availability. For Beacon, site users see only their own site's rows.
A temporary need for moving from the current state to the new one, such as knowledge articles for the service desk or retiring the emailed extracts.
A prioritization scheme: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have this time. Must items define the minimum acceptable release.
The first stage of the ITIL Version 5 product and service lifecycle, where consumer needs, outcomes and demand are understood before design.

build.goal: Open the requirements and traceability register for Release 1 with an elicitation summary, the needs you draw out from emergency and patient-flow leaders, the agreed KPI definitions and privacy constraints, each with an ID, source, priority and testable acceptance criterion.
steps: Open Project, Release 1, Requirements and traceability register. Read How to write it and See the finished example.

Write the elicitation summary: who you spoke to (with E-IDs), how (interview, workshop, observation, document analysis, questionnaire, prototype) and when, inside 2026-09-01 to 2026-09-08, plus the main findings.

Use the interview guide above with Janelle Cardinal and run the KPI definitions workshop. Record what you learn as findings, for example that sites did not agree when the wait clock starts and that 34.0% of visits arrive between 17:00 and 23:59.

In the requirements register, record at least ten requirements, one per row: ID (REQ-01 onward), requirement, source (person and E-ID), MoSCoW priority, acceptance criterion and status. Cover measures, access, privacy, support and accessibility, and decide each one's type (business, stakeholder, functional, non-functional, transition) so you know how it will be tested.
Record the KPI definitions (clock start, time to PIA, ED length of stay, LWBS, % within CTAS objective) as requirements owned by Dr. Whitford.

Add requirements for the privacy constraints, the Health Information Act least-amount and highest-anonymity duties and Kestrel's suppress-under-5 rule, sourced from Priya Raman (E-003), and an open data questions table for anything only a data owner can answer. Leave the traceability matrix for tomorrow.
build.modelAnswer: A strong register opening reads as an elicitation summary plus a clean list. Each requirement states one need in testable words, names a real source with an E-ID, and has a priority and an acceptance criterion. KPI definitions match Kestrel's: clock from arrival, LWBS as left before a physician initial assessment. Privacy constraints are rows of their own, not footnotes.

examTips.tip: People task 5 Align stakeholder expectations: when stakeholders disagree on a definition or priority, the best answer brings them together to agree it (a facilitated workshop), not the PM choosing or escalating first.

Process task 2 Develop and manage project scope starts with requirements. Expect to match techniques to situations: observation for tacit work, workshops for cross-group agreement, prototypes when users cannot describe what they want.
Guiding principle Start where you are: before replacing a process or tool, assess what exists and reuse what works. An answer that discards everything and starts fresh is usually wrong.

Value co-creation: questions often contrast a provider deciding what consumers need with consumers and providers defining outcomes together. Pick the collaborative answer tied to the consumer's outcomes.

pitfalls: Recording solutions as requirements. Send the extract at 06:00 is a solution; know which site is behind before the huddle is the need.
Interviewing only senior leaders. Charge nurses and unit clerks know where the data comes from and how it is really used.
Leaving definitions open. Two sites with two clocks will never reconcile; get one definition signed by the data owner.
Writing untestable words such as fast or user-friendly. If you cannot write the test, you cannot accept the requirement.

check.q: Janelle Cardinal says, 'Just email me the extract an hour earlier.' What do you do with that request?
check.a: Treat it as a proposed solution and ask about the need behind it: what decision she makes, when, and with which numbers. The requirement is likely to know each site's ED and bed pressure before the morning huddle, which the dashboard can meet without emailing patient detail.

check.q: Why is observing the KGH morning bed huddle worth the time when you have already interviewed the director?
check.a: Interviews capture what people believe they do; observation shows what they actually do and the tacit steps they never mention. It reveals which numbers are used, when, and by whom, so requirements match real work.

check.q: Why is 'Confirm requirements and KPI definitions' a risk to the Release 1 gate?
check.a: It is task 3 on the critical path, with six working days from 2026-09-01 to 2026-09-08 and zero float. Any delay pushes the privacy impact assessment, the warehouse build and every later critical task, so the 2026-10-23 gate moves unless time is recovered elsewhere.

items.summary: You learn how a scope statement fixes what Release 1 delivers and excludes, how to write acceptance criteria that a DAX measure can prove, and how traceability links each need to design, test and acceptance. You write the scope statement and complete the traceability columns.

read.heading: The scope statement
read.body:
The scope statement turns the charter's high-level scope into a precise description that the team builds to and the business accepts against. It has six parts:
1. Product scope description: what Release 1 is. A de-identified Power BI service with an emergency department (ED) flow report and a bed occupancy report, built on the Beacon semantic model with row-level security (RLS) by site, supported by the service desk.
2. Deliverables: the semantic model, reports, de-identified warehouse views, RLS test pack, support handover and their documents.
3. Acceptance criteria: the measurable conditions for each deliverable.
4. Exclusions: what Release 1 will not do.
5. Constraints: the 2026-10-23 gate, the CAD 420,000 Release 1 budget, Health Information Act (HIA) duties, Kestrel's small-count rule.
6. Assumptions: for example, that the Clinical Data Warehouse (A-010) can host the de-identified views and that the business owners attend user acceptance testing (UAT) from 2026-10-21 to 2026-10-23.

Product scope describes the features of the result; project scope is the work needed to deliver it, including the privacy impact assessment, testing and training. The scope statement, the work breakdown structure (WBS) and its dictionary together form the scope baseline.

read.heading: Exclusions and scope control
read.body:
Exclusions prevent arguments later. Release 1 excludes:
- Patient names, health numbers, dates of birth or bed numbers, on any page or in the model.
- Changes to the source systems, such as the ED Tracking Board (A-002) and the Bed Management System (A-006), or to the Clinical Information System (CIS); Beacon reads from them.
- DirectQuery or real-time pages; Release 1 uses scheduled Import refresh.
- Forecasting models of ED demand.
- Identity, access and resilience work, which belongs to Releases 2 and 3.

Two failures threaten scope. Scope creep is uncontrolled growth, often one small request at a time. Gold plating is the team adding extras nobody asked for, such as a forecasting page, because they can. Both add cost and risk without approval. Once the scope baseline is approved, every addition goes through the change-control board chaired by Marcus Bell (E-002), with its impact on schedule, cost, privacy and security assessed first. The answer may still be yes; the point is that it is decided, not drifted into.

read.heading: Acceptance criteria
read.body:
Acceptance criteria are the conditions a deliverable must meet before the owner accepts it. Write them so a tester and the business owner would reach the same verdict. A useful form is Given, When, Then.

| Requirement | Acceptance criterion |
|---|---|
| ED page shows median minutes to physician initial assessment (PIA) by site | Given the cleaned Q3 data, when the page is filtered to KGH, then the median shows 80.5 minutes, matching the approved figure |
| Show the left without being seen (LWBS) rate by site | Given Q3 data, when no site filter is applied, then the rate shows 5.7% (27 of 474 valid visits) |
| Site users see only their own site | Given a user in the ARH role, when they open the report, then only ARH rows appear, and a negative test confirms KGH rows are hidden |
| Small counts are protected | Given a page shared outside the care team, when a count is under 5, then it is suppressed, and a rate whose numerator is under 5 is blank |

The small-count criterion is not theoretical. Computed from the cleaned extract, Q3 LWBS counts were KGH 16, ARH 5, CVH 4 and PGH 2, so the CVH and PGH LWBS counts must be suppressed, and their LWBS rates blanked, on pages shared outside the care team. Medians are not suppressed by this rule.

Acceptance criteria differ from a definition of done. Done is the team's general quality bar for any item; acceptance criteria are specific to one deliverable and agreed with its owner.

read.heading: From requirement to measure
read.body:
In Power BI a requirement becomes a measure, and the acceptance criterion becomes a test of that measure. These three come from Kestrel's DAX starters and use the real model names:

```
ED Visits =
COUNTROWS ( FactEDVisit )

Median Minutes to PIA =
MEDIANX (
    FILTER ( FactEDVisit, NOT ISBLANK ( FactEDVisit[MinutesToPIA] ) ),
    FactEDVisit[MinutesToPIA]
)

LWBS Rate =
DIVIDE (
    CALCULATE ( [ED Visits], FactEDVisit[Disposition] = "LWBS" ),
    [ED Visits]
)
```

MEDIANX over a FILTER drops visits with no valid time, so LWBS visits and the nulled rows V0385 and V0421 stay out of the median. DIVIDE returns blank instead of an error when a site has no visits.

Test them in DAX query view in Power BI Desktop:

```
EVALUATE
SUMMARIZECOLUMNS (
    DimSite[SiteCode],
    "Visits", [ED Visits],
    "LWBS Rate", [LWBS Rate],
    "Median Minutes to PIA", [Median Minutes to PIA]
)
ORDER BY DimSite[SiteCode]
```

The result must match the approved figures: ARH 105 visits, 4.8%, 54.5 minutes; CVH 101, 4.0%, 54.0; KGH 213, 7.5%, 80.5; PGH 55, 3.6%, 45.5. A mismatch is a defect to trace before acceptance, never a number to explain away.

read.heading: Traceability
read.body:
A traceability register links every requirement to where it came from and where it ends up. Typical columns: requirement ID, source (person or document), business objective, statement, priority, design element (measure, visual or RLS role), test case ID, acceptance status.

Beacon's traceability matrix traces each requirement forward to the design, the work package and schedule task that build it, and the test that proves it:

| Requirement | Design | Build | Test evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| REQ-01 One time-to-PIA definition, Dr. Whitford (E-007) | Median Minutes to PIA in the DAX catalogue; ED page | WP-104, task 8 | 64.0 minutes overall and 80.5 at KGH; UAT, task 11 |
| REQ-02 LWBS rate by site and month, Dr. Whitford (E-007) | LWBS Rate measure | WP-104, task 8 | 5.7% overall, KGH 7.5% |
| REQ-07 Each site sees only its own data, Daniel Osei (E-004) and Janelle Cardinal (E-008) | RLS roles by site | WP-104, task 9 | RLS test pack, positive and negative tests |
| REQ-08 No direct identifiers; counts under 5 suppressed, Priya Raman (E-003) | Classification register; privacy impact assessment | WP-102, task 4; WP-103, task 6 | Small-count cases: CVH and PGH LWBS counts hidden, rates blank |

Traceability runs both ways. Forward, from requirement to design and test, shows nothing was forgotten. Backward, from a feature to its requirement, exposes gold plating: a page with no requirement behind it. When a change request arrives, the register shows which designs and tests it touches, which is the start of its impact assessment.

read.heading: Control quality, then validate scope
read.body:
Two checks happen before acceptance, and the exam keeps them apart.
- Control quality is internal: the team checks the work is correct, for example by reconciling every measure to the approved figures and running the RLS tests.
- Validate scope is external: the business owners formally accept the deliverables against the agreed criteria. In Beacon that is task 11, UAT with ED and patient-flow leaders, 2026-10-21 to 2026-10-23, on the critical path.

Control quality usually comes first, so owners review work that already passes the team's checks. Accepted deliverables, with signed acceptance criteria, are the evidence the Release 1 go-live gate needs on 2026-10-23.

keyTerms.definition: Describes product scope, deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions, constraints and assumptions. With the WBS and WBS dictionary it forms the scope baseline.
Specific, measurable conditions one deliverable must meet before its owner accepts it, such as the KGH median reconciling to 80.5 minutes.
Uncontrolled growth in scope without assessing impact or getting approval, often through many small requests.
The team adding features nobody asked for. It adds cost and risk and is caught by backward traceability.
Linking each requirement to its source, design element, test and acceptance status, forward and backward, so gaps and extras are visible.
Formal acceptance of completed deliverables by the customer or sponsor, after the team's own quality control.
A Power BI Desktop view for running DAX queries such as EVALUATE SUMMARIZECOLUMNS, used here to test measures against approved figures.

build.goal: Write the Release 1 scope statement with product scope, deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions, constraints and assumptions, and complete the requirements and traceability register with design elements, tests and acceptance status.
steps: Open Project, Release 1, Scope statement. Read How to write it and See the finished example.

Write the product scope description in a short paragraph that names the systems with asset IDs, Import storage mode, scheduled refresh through the gateway, RLS and the Confidential label. Then list the deliverables with IDs and work packages (DEL-01 to DEL-07, WP-102 to WP-105) and at least four exclusions.
List constraints (gate 2026-10-23, CAD 420,000, HIA duties, suppress-under-5 rule) and at least three assumptions, each with an owner who can confirm it.

Write a pass or fail acceptance criterion and its evidence for each area (data, ED measures, bed measures, access, privacy, quality, service), using approved figures: 474 valid visits, KGH 80.5 minutes, 5.7% LWBS, 87.0% average occupancy, ARH-only RLS, suppression of the CVH and PGH LWBS counts. Given, When, Then wording helps keep each one testable.

Write the acceptance process: evidence filed before UAT; UAT as task 11 (2026-10-21 to 2026-10-23); Grace Liu (E-005) accepts the service into support; the business owners accept the results; and Dr. Helen Marchetti decides at the go-live gate, task 12, on 2026-10-23.

Open Requirements and traceability register. Add the acceptance criterion and status to each requirement, then build the traceability matrix: design, build (work package and schedule task) and test evidence.
If you have the model from the labs, run the DAX query from the lesson in DAX query view and record the result against each test; otherwise record the expected values.
Check backward traceability: list any planned page or feature with no requirement, and remove it or raise it as a change.
build.modelAnswer: A strong scope statement makes exclusions as clear as inclusions and has a measurable criterion for every deliverable. The register links each requirement to a named source, a measure or RLS role, and a test with an expected value from the approved figures, such as KGH 80.5 minutes. No feature lacks a requirement.

examTips.tip: Process task 2 Develop and manage project scope: the scope baseline is the scope statement, WBS and WBS dictionary. If a team member adds an unrequested feature, the issue is gold plating; the response is to stop it and, if valuable, route it through change control.

Validate scope is customer acceptance; control quality is the team's correctness check. When a question asks how deliverables become accepted, choose validate scope with the agreed acceptance criteria.

Model the data, create model calculations using DAX: know that DIVIDE handles divide-by-zero safely, that CALCULATE changes filter context (as in LWBS Rate), and that DAX query view lets you test measures with EVALUATE.

pitfalls: Writing acceptance criteria as feelings. 'Leaders are happy with the ED page' cannot be tested; 'KGH median shows 80.5 minutes' can.
Skipping exclusions. If patient-level lists are not explicitly excluded, someone will assume they are coming.
Tracing only forward. Backward traceability is what catches gold plating and features nobody owns.
Explaining away a reconciliation gap. If a measure does not match the approved figure, trace the cause before acceptance.

check.q: What is the difference between product scope and project scope for Release 1?
check.a: Product scope is the features of the result: the de-identified ED and bed reports, the semantic model with RLS by site and the supported service. Project scope is all the work to deliver it, including the privacy impact assessment, data cleaning, testing, training and the support handover.

check.q: Why must the CVH and PGH LWBS counts be suppressed on pages shared outside the care team?
check.a: Computed from the cleaned Q3 extract, CVH had 4 and PGH had 2 LWBS visits. Kestrel's policy suppresses counts under 5 in any report shared outside the care team, and blanks any rate whose numerator is under 5, so their LWBS rates are blank too, because small counts can help identify patients, which is also why R-02 is in the RAID log.

check.q: Your DAX query shows KGH's median minutes to PIA as 82.0, not 80.5. What do you do?
check.a: Treat it as a defect and trace it before acceptance. Check the cleaning rules (duplicates removed, V0385 and V0421 nulled, quarantined rows excluded), the measure logic and the clock (arrival, not triage). Fix the cause and re-run until it reconciles.

items.summary: You learn to decompose the programme into a work breakdown structure and to find the critical path with a forward and backward pass. You build the Beacon WBS from the programme register and the schedule from khn_schedule.csv in Microsoft Project, with float and the three gates.

read.heading: The WBS: decompose by deliverable
read.body:
A work breakdown structure (WBS) breaks the total scope into smaller, manageable pieces. Each level down is more detailed; the lowest level is the work package, which can be estimated, scheduled, costed and given one owner. The 100% rule says the WBS contains all the scope and nothing outside it, and each level adds up exactly to its parent. A WBS dictionary describes each work package: scope, deliverables, owner, budget, acceptance criteria.

Beacon decomposes programme, then release, then 15 work packages (from khn_programme_register.csv after cleaning):

| WP | Release | Work package | Owner | Budget CAD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WP-101 | 1 | Programme mobilization and charter | Programme Manager | 40,000 |
| WP-102 | 1 | Privacy impact assessment and threat model | E-003 | 70,000 |
| WP-103 | 1 | Source profiling, data quality and warehouse staging | E-013 | 130,000 |
| WP-104 | 1 | Semantic model, dashboards and row-level security | E-006 | 140,000 |
| WP-105 | 1 | Service transition and service desk readiness | E-005 | 40,000 |
| WP-106 | 2 | Role catalogue and RBAC (role-based access control) design | E-004 | 90,000 |
| WP-107 | 2 | Joiner-mover-leaver integration with HR | E-018 | 110,000 |
| WP-108 | 2 | MFA (multi-factor authentication) and single sign-on rollout | None recorded | 130,000 |
| WP-109 | 2 | Privileged access and segregation of duties | E-004 | 70,000 |
| WP-110 | 2 | Access-request value stream and access reviews | E-005 | 60,000 |
| WP-111 | 3 | Business impact analysis and recovery targets | E-016 | 55,000 |
| WP-112 | 3 | Clinical Information System (CIS) restore testing and downtime procedures | E-016 | 85,000 |
| WP-113 | 3 | Incident response plan and tabletop exercise | E-004 | 60,000 |
| WP-114 | 3 | Vulnerability remediation and security operations dashboard | E-020 | 80,000 |
| WP-115 | 3 | Major-incident review and programme closure | Programme Manager | 40,000 |

The releases add to 420,000, 460,000 and 320,000: CAD 1,200,000. Summing raw rows gives 1,220,000 (WP-104 appears twice); removing only the duplicate gives 1,080,000 (WP-113 is stored as -60,000, a sign error finance confirmed). WP-108 has no owner, so the sponsor must name one.

read.heading: From work packages to a network
read.body:
Work packages break into activities, and activities are linked by dependencies:
- Finish-to-start (FS): B starts after A finishes. The most common, and the only type in Beacon.
- Start-to-start (SS), finish-to-finish (FF) and start-to-finish (SF, rare).

A dependency can be mandatory (built into the work: you cannot test RLS before the model exists), discretionary (a team choice), external (outside the project, such as a vendor delivery) or internal. A lead lets a successor start early; a lag adds waiting time. Milestones have zero duration and mark events: Beacon's are task 2 Charter approved, 12 Release 1 go-live gate, 20 Release 2 acceptance gate and 28 Programme acceptance.

khn_schedule.csv has 28 rows: row 1 is the programme summary (78 days, starting 2026-09-01) and 27 tasks follow, with durations in working days, predecessors, resource names and the release. Only row 1 carries a start date; every other date comes from the links and a Monday to Friday calendar. Task names use ED for emergency department, KPI for key performance indicator, RLS for row-level security and UAT for user acceptance testing.

read.heading: The forward pass
read.body:
The forward pass finds the earliest start (ES) and earliest finish (EF) of every task. Using working-day numbers, where day 1 is Tuesday 2026-09-01:
- A task with no predecessor starts on day 1.
- EF = ES + duration - 1.
- ES = the largest EF among its predecessors + 1.
- A milestone takes the largest EF of its predecessors.

Release 1 worked through:

| ID | Task | Days | After | ES to EF | Dates |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | Confirm requirements and KPI definitions | 6 | 2 | 1 to 6 | 09-01 to 09-08 |
| 4 | Complete privacy impact assessment | 12 | 3 | 7 to 18 | 09-09 to 09-24 |
| 5 | Profile and clean ED and bed sources | 10 | 3 | 7 to 16 | 09-09 to 09-22 |
| 7 | Threat model the analytics architecture | 7 | 3 | 7 to 13 | 09-09 to 09-17 |
| 6 | Warehouse staging and de-identified views | 8 | 4, 5 | 19 to 26 | 09-25 to 10-06 |
| 8 | Semantic model and DAX measures | 7 | 6 | 27 to 33 | 10-07 to 10-15 |
| 9 | Configure RLS and sensitivity labels | 3 | 7, 8 | 34 to 36 | 10-16 to 10-20 |
| 10 | Service desk support and knowledge | 4 | 8 | 34 to 37 | 10-16 to 10-21 |
| 11 | UAT with ED and patient-flow leaders | 3 | 9 | 37 to 39 | 10-21 to 10-23 |
| 12 | Release 1 go-live gate | 0 | 10, 11 | 39 | 10-23 |

Task 6 waits for the later of tasks 4 (day 18) and 5 (day 16), so it starts on day 19. The privacy impact assessment, not the data work, drives the start of the warehouse build.

read.heading: The backward pass and float
read.body:
The backward pass finds the latest finish (LF) and latest start (LS) that do not delay the end date, working from the last task back:
- The final task's LF equals its EF.
- LF = the smallest LS among its successors - 1.
- LS = LF - duration + 1.
- A task whose successor is a milestone takes the milestone's day as its LF, because a milestone has no duration (task 10 feeds gate 12 on day 39).

Total float = LS - ES: how long a task can slip without moving the programme finish. Free float: how long it can slip without delaying any successor's early start.

| ID | LS to LF (days) | Total float | Free float | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | 36 to 39 | 2 | 2 | Gate needs it by day 39; it ends day 37 |
| 9 | 34 to 36 | 0 | 0 | UAT starts day 37 |
| 5 | 9 to 18 | 2 | 2 | Task 6 cannot start before day 19 anyway |
| 7 | 21 to 27 | 14 | 0 | See below |
| 4 | 7 to 18 | 0 | 0 | Drives task 6 |

Task 7 is the lesson. It feeds task 9 (late start day 34) and task 13, Design role catalogue and RBAC model (late start day 28, 2026-10-08). Its LF is the smaller of 33 and 27, so 27 (2026-10-07), giving a late start of day 21 (2026-09-29) and total float of 14. Forget a successor and you would wrongly give it 20 days. Its free float is 0 because task 13 can start the very next day, 2026-09-18.

read.heading: Beacon's critical path and gates
read.body:
The critical path is the longest path through the network; its tasks have zero total float, so any slip moves the finish. Beacon's runs 2 > 3 > 4 > 6 > 8 > 9 > 11 > 12 > 14 > 17 > 19 > 20 > 21 > 22 > 26 > 27 > 28, giving 78 working days from 2026-09-01 to 2026-12-17. The gates fall out of the forward pass: Release 1 go-live 2026-10-23, Release 2 acceptance 2026-11-26, programme acceptance 2026-12-17.

Tasks with float: 5 (2 days), 7 (14), 10 (2), 13 (14), 15 (4), 16 (6), 18 (4), 23 (1), 24 (2), 25 (2). Task 23, the tabletop exercise, has 1 day: near-critical, so watch it.

Calendars matter. Kestrel's file has no holidays. Computed by adding Thanksgiving (2026-10-12) and Remembrance Day (2026-11-11) as non-working days: the Release 1 gate moves to 2026-10-26, Release 2 to 2026-11-30 and programme acceptance to 2026-12-21, because both days fall on critical tasks. Confirm Kestrel's calendar before you baseline.

To shorten a critical path: crashing adds resources to critical tasks and costs more; fast tracking overlaps tasks planned in sequence and adds risk. Both only help on the critical path.

read.heading: Building it in Microsoft Project
read.body:
1. Create a blank project. On the Project tab choose Project Information and set the start date to 2026-09-01 before you import.
2. Open khn_schedule.csv (choose CSV as the file type). In the Import Wizard create a new map, append the data to the active project, and map Name, Duration, Start, Predecessors, Resource Names and Milestone. Put Release in a spare text field such as Text1.
3. Select rows 2 to 28 and choose Task, Indent Task, so row 1 becomes the summary. Its duration should read 78 days.
4. Check the calendar under Project, Change Working Time: Monday to Friday. Add holidays only if Kestrel confirms them, and record the effect on the gates.
5. On the Gantt Chart Format tab tick Critical Tasks. Insert the Total Slack and Free Slack columns; Microsoft Project calls float slack. Compare with the lesson: task 7 shows 14 days total slack.
6. When the sponsor accepts it, choose Project, Set Baseline, so later progress is measured against it.

Then export a milestone list with the four milestones and their dates for the status dashboard.

keyTerms.definition: The lowest level of the WBS: work that can be estimated, scheduled, costed and assigned to one owner, such as WP-104 Semantic model, dashboards and row-level security.
The WBS includes all of the scope and nothing else, and each level adds up exactly to its parent, including the budget.
The longest path through the schedule network. Its tasks have zero total float, so any delay on them delays the finish.
How long a task can slip without moving the project finish: late start minus early start. Microsoft Project calls it Total Slack.
How long a task can slip without delaying the early start of any successor.
Running critical tasks in parallel that were planned in sequence. Saves time but adds rework risk.
Adding resources to critical tasks to shorten them. Saves time but costs more.

build.goal: Build the Beacon work breakdown structure from the cleaned programme register and the Microsoft Project schedule from khn_schedule.csv, then record the critical path, float and the three gates.
steps: Open Project, Release 1, Work breakdown structure. Read How to write it and See the finished example.

In Practice, Labs, download khn_programme_register.csv. Remove the WP-104 duplicate, take the absolute value of WP-113, repair WP-109's impossible finish (2026-11-31) to 2026-11-04 from schedule task 16, cap WP-101 at 100%, fix the casing, and confirm the releases total 420,000, 460,000 and 320,000.

Write the WBS as programme, release and work package with WBS codes (1.1.1 onward), a dictionary row per work package (owner, budget, dates and main outputs), the budget roll-up with the reserve outside the WBS, and the link from every schedule task to its work package. Flag WP-108's missing owner for the sponsor.
Download khn_schedule.csv from the Microsoft Project schedule lab and import it as the lesson describes: start date 2026-09-01 first, then the Import Wizard, then indent rows 2 to 28.
Show Critical Tasks and the Total Slack and Free Slack columns. Check the critical path and the floats against the lesson, especially task 7 (14 total, 0 free).
Open Microsoft Project schedule in Project. Record the critical path, the float table, the three gates and the calendar note on Thanksgiving and Remembrance Day.
Set the baseline in Microsoft Project, then complete Done when and Check yourself for both documents.
build.modelAnswer: A good WBS shows three releases and 15 work packages whose budgets add to CAD 1,200,000, each with a dictionary entry and an owner or a flagged gap. The schedule document lists the critical path from task 2 to 28, the float of every non-critical task, gates on 2026-10-23, 2026-11-26 and 2026-12-17, and the calendar risk.

examTips.tip: Process task 8 Plan and manage schedule: expect forward and backward pass questions. Remember EF = ES + duration - 1 with day numbers, LF comes from the smallest successor LS, and a task with several successors takes its float from the tightest one.
When asked to recover schedule, look at the critical path first. Fast tracking adds risk, crashing adds cost; adding people to a task with float does nothing for the finish date.
Process task 2 Develop and manage project scope: the WBS is deliverable-oriented and obeys the 100% rule. Activities and dates belong to the schedule, not the WBS itself.

pitfalls: Importing before setting the project start date. Microsoft Project then schedules from today and every date is wrong.
Leaving row 1 as an ordinary task. Indent rows 2 to 28 so it becomes the summary; otherwise it sits in the network and distorts the critical path.
Taking float from one successor only. Task 7 has 14 days of float because of task 13, not 20 because of task 9.
Totalling budgets from raw rows. The duplicate and the sign error turn CAD 1,200,000 into 1,220,000 or 1,080,000.

check.q: Why does task 6, Build warehouse staging and de-identified views, start on 2026-09-25 and not 2026-09-23?
check.a: It has two finish-to-start predecessors: task 5 finishes on day 16 (2026-09-22) and task 4, the privacy impact assessment, on day 18 (2026-09-24). A task starts after the latest predecessor finishes, so task 6 starts on day 19, 2026-09-25. Task 4 is the driver and is critical.

check.q: Task 5, Profile and clean ED and bed census sources, slips by three days. What happens to the Release 1 gate?
check.a: Task 5 has 2 days of total float. A three-day slip uses the float and pushes task 6 one day, and because task 6 is critical, every later critical task and the 2026-10-23 gate move one working day, to 2026-10-26, unless time is recovered.

check.q: What is the difference between task 7's total float of 14 days and its free float of 0?
check.a: Total float says task 7 can slip 14 working days before the programme finish moves, because its latest finish is set by task 13's late start on 2026-10-08. Free float of 0 says any slip at all delays task 13's early start, since task 13 is planned to begin the next working day.

items.summary: You learn to identify and analyze stakeholders by power, interest and engagement, and to plan communication that fits each audience. You build Beacon's stakeholder register and communication plan for clinical, privacy, security, support and vendor stakeholders.

read.heading: Identify everyone who is affected
read.body:
A stakeholder is anyone who affects, is affected by, or believes they are affected by the programme. Missing one is expensive: the person you forgot is often the one who blocks go-live.

Find them from the charter, the organization chart, the data owners and the systems touched. For Beacon, think in groups:
- Executives: Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001), sponsor; Marcus Bell (E-002), CIO (Chief Information Officer) and change-control chair.
- Privacy and security: Priya Raman (E-003), Daniel Osei (E-004), Sam Okafor (E-020).
- Data owners and leaders: Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007), Janelle Cardinal (E-008).
- Frontline users: Aisha Mahmoud (E-010), Ben Kowalski (E-011), Dr. Liam O'Connor (E-012).
- Delivery and support: Tomás Rivera (E-006), Mei Tanaka (E-013), Grace Liu (E-005), Kevin Park (E-009), Ahmed Haddad (E-017), Nora Lindqvist (E-018), Chloe Dubois (E-016).
- Vendors: Meridian Clinical Systems (V-01), NorthArc Cloud (V-02), ClearPath Staffing (V-03), Sentinel SOC Services (V-04), Lumen Analytics Partners (V-05).
- External: the Information and Privacy Commissioner, who reviews and comments on the privacy impact assessment. Patients are affected but not consulted directly in Release 1.

A stakeholder register records, for each person or group: ID, name and role, interest in Beacon, power or influence, expectations, current and desired engagement, and the approach you will take.

read.heading: Analyze power, interest and engagement
read.body:
A power-interest grid places each stakeholder by how much they can affect the programme and how much they care:

| | Low interest | High interest |
|---|---|---|
| High power | Keep satisfied | Manage closely |
| Low power | Monitor | Keep informed |

Grids drift, so review them at each release.

The engagement assessment matrix records where each stakeholder is now (C) and where you need them (D), on five levels:
- Unaware: does not know about Beacon or its impact.
- Resistant: aware and opposed to the change.
- Neutral: aware, neither supportive nor resistant.
- Supportive: aware and in favour.
- Leading: aware and actively helping it succeed.

The gap between C and D is your work. Not everyone needs to be Leading: a vendor can be Supportive, and so can a data owner who agrees the definitions and signs off the tests. Janelle Cardinal, the main user, should lead, because the dashboards only work if someone in the business champions them to the sites.

read.heading: Beacon's key stakeholders
read.body:
This is your analysis, not data. Engagement levels are judgments you revisit.

| Stakeholder | Power, interest | Current to desired | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dr. Helen Marchetti (E-001) | High, high | Leading to Leading | Weekly check-in with decisions ready |
| Marcus Bell (E-002) | High, high | Supportive to Leading | Chairs the board; a cost recovery plan before any reserve request (R-08) |
| Priya Raman (E-003) | High, high | Supportive to Leading | Early review of de-identified views; co-owns the small-count tests; owns R-02 and R-05 |
| Daniel Osei (E-004) | High, high | Supportive to Supportive | Threat model and row-level security (RLS) tests; owns R-04 |
| Dr. Sarah Whitford (E-007) | High, high | Neutral to Supportive | Owns emergency department (ED) definitions; agree the time-to-PIA definition and show the model reproducing 80.5 minutes; she signs off key performance indicators and user acceptance testing |
| Janelle Cardinal (E-008) | High, high | Supportive to Leading | Main user; co-designs the bed pages and leads UAT; owns R-03 |
| Aisha Mahmoud (E-010) | Low, high | Unaware to Supportive | Keep informed; test page design with her |
| Kevin Park (E-009) | Medium, medium | Neutral to Supportive | Expect concern when Release 2 removes his conflicting rights (I-01); explain why early |

Look at the patterns. Everyone in Manage closely has a decision or a risk to own. Frontline users have little power but decide whether the dashboards get used, so their interest must be turned into support.

read.heading: Planning communication
read.body:
A communication plan says who needs what information, why, when, through which channel, from whom, and how you will know it landed. Three methods:
- Push: you send it (status report, email). Good for many readers; no proof it was read.
- Pull: they fetch it when needed (the Project page, a knowledge article). Good for large audiences and reference.
- Interactive: two-way, in real time (meetings, workshops, huddles). Best for decisions, conflict and complex topics.

Communication load grows quickly. Channels = n(n - 1) / 2. Beacon's 19 named people (E-001 to E-018 and E-020, including an agency nurse and a vendor engineer) plus you make 20 people, so 20 x 19 / 2 = 190 possible channels (computed). Add one person and you add 20 channels. That is why the plan names one owner per audience instead of everyone talking to everyone.

Tailor by audience. The sponsor wants decisions, money and risks on one page. Data owners want definitions and evidence. Frontline staff want what changes for them and when. Vendors need scope, dates and contract terms. Plan feedback too: a briefing without questions is a broadcast.

read.heading: Beacon's communication plan
read.body:
| Communication | Audience | Owner | Method | When |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sponsor check-in | E-001 | Programme Manager | Meeting (interactive) | Weekly, Monday |
| Status report | E-001 to E-005 | Programme Manager | Report in the library, email notice (push) | Weekly, Friday |
| Change-control board | Board members | Marcus Bell (E-002) | Meeting; decisions into the RAID log | Every two weeks and on demand |
| Release 1 working group | E-006, E-007, E-008, E-013 | Tomás Rivera | Meeting with a live model demo | Weekly during build |
| Data-quality exceptions | E-007, E-008 | Tomás Rivera | Exception list from the workbook (push) | When a refresh quarantines rows |
| Privacy and security review | E-003, E-004 | Programme Manager | Workshop (interactive) | Before each gate |
| Service desk briefing | E-005 and analysts | Grace Liu | Briefing and knowledge articles | Task 10, 2026-10-16 to 2026-10-21 |
| Go-live notice | Dashboard users at all four sites | Janelle Cardinal | Email and huddle script | After the gate on 2026-10-23 |
| Vendor check-in | V-01, V-04, V-05 | Programme Manager | Meeting | Every two weeks |
| Programme news | All Kestrel staff | Dr. Helen Marchetti | Intranet article (pull) | At each gate |

Cadences and owners are agreed with the sponsor. The go-live notice comes from Janelle Cardinal, not the programme, because people trust messages from their own leaders. The RAID log is the risks, assumptions, issues and decisions log you open tomorrow.

read.heading: The ITIL view: relationships and visibility
read.body:
ITIL treats stakeholders as partners in co-creating value. The analytics service's value depends on leaders using it, the service desk supporting it and privacy staff trusting it. Three guiding principles apply:
- Collaborate and promote visibility: share the draft definitions, test results and risks openly. Hidden work breeds distrust, especially after years of extracts that disagreed.
- Focus on value: frame every message by the outcome for that audience, such as fewer patients leaving unseen for ED leaders.
- Think and work holistically: the dashboards, the data sources, the support model and the people form one service, so no group can be left out of the plan.

In PMP terms, today practises People tasks 4 Engage stakeholders, 5 Align stakeholder expectations, 6 Manage stakeholder expectations and 8 Plan and manage communication. In practice they are one loop: identify, analyze, plan, engage, then check whether engagement moved from current to desired.

keyTerms.definition: A record of each stakeholder's role, interest, power, expectations, current and desired engagement, and the approach to engage them.
A two-by-two that sorts stakeholders into manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed and monitor.
Shows each stakeholder's current (C) and desired (D) engagement on five levels: Unaware, Resistant, Neutral, Supportive, Leading.
The number of possible two-way links in a group, n(n - 1) / 2. For Beacon's 20 people it is 190.
Communication methods: you send (push), they fetch (pull), or you exchange in real time (interactive). Use interactive for decisions and conflict.
States for each audience what they need, why, the channel, the frequency, the owner and how feedback is collected.

build.goal: Build the Beacon stakeholder register with power, interest and engagement for each stakeholder, and a communication plan that matches message, channel, frequency and owner to each audience.
steps: Open Project, Release 1, Stakeholder register. Read How to write it and See the finished example.
List every stakeholder from the lesson's groups, including the five vendors and the Information and Privacy Commissioner, with ID, role and interest in Beacon.
Rate power and interest, place each on the power-interest grid and record current and desired engagement using the five levels.
Write one engagement approach per stakeholder, linking the risk or decision they own (for example R-03 for Janelle Cardinal, R-04 for Daniel Osei).

Open Communication plan. Write the goals and principles, the audiences and their needs, then the communication matrix: communication, audience, owner, method (push, pull or interactive) and when. Add the weekly status report format with its red, amber and green rules.

Add the channels calculation (20 people, 190 channels), the escalation routes (an issue unresolved in 2 working days goes to the Programme Manager, then the sponsor; a suspected privacy breach goes to Priya Raman at once; a security incident goes to Sam Okafor, then Daniel Osei), what must never appear in a message, and how you will know messages landed. Complete Done when and Check yourself for both documents.
build.modelAnswer: A strong register covers executives, data owners, privacy, security, frontline, support, vendors and the Commissioner, with a reason for every rating and a C to D gap that the approach addresses. The communication plan gives each audience one owner, a fitting method and a feedback route, and frontline messages come from their own leaders.

examTips.tip: People task 4 Engage stakeholders: when a stakeholder resists, the first move is to understand their concern directly, not to escalate or go around them. The engagement assessment matrix (Unaware, Resistant, Neutral, Supportive, Leading) appears often.

People task 8 Plan and manage communication: know n(n - 1) / 2. If a team grows from 10 to 12 people, channels rise from 45 to 66. Choose interactive communication for urgent, complex or sensitive messages.
Collaborate and promote visibility: answers that make work, risks and progress visible to stakeholders beat answers that keep information inside the delivery team, even when the news is bad.

pitfalls: Treating the register as a contact list. Without power, interest, engagement and an approach, it cannot guide action.
Sending everyone the same report. The sponsor, the charge nurse and the vendor need different content and channels.
Forgetting low-power, high-interest users. Frontline staff cannot stop the release, but they decide whether it gets used.
Planning push only. Status emails do not resolve disagreement; decisions and conflict need interactive channels.

check.q: Where does Aisha Mahmoud (E-010) sit on the power-interest grid, and how should you engage her?
check.a: Low power, high interest: keep informed. She cannot stop the release, but she uses ED data every shift, so test page designs with her, brief her through her own leader and move her from Unaware to Supportive before go-live.

check.q: Beacon has 20 people. How many communication channels is that, and why does it matter?
check.a: 20 x 19 / 2 = 190 channels. So many paths make messages drift and contradict each other, so the plan gives each audience one owner and one main channel instead of everyone talking to everyone.

check.q: Why should frontline briefings come from Janelle Cardinal rather than the programme?
check.a: People trust messages from their own leader, and she owns the bed data and is the main dashboard user. A briefing from her shows the change is hers, not something done to her teams, which supports adoption.

items.summary: You learn to log and manage risks, assumptions, issues and decisions, choose risk responses, use reserves, and run changes through a change-control board. You open Beacon's RAID log with R-01 to R-08, I-01 to I-03 and D-01, and set up the change-control process.

read.heading: RAID: four kinds of entry
read.body:
A RAID log keeps Risks, Assumptions, Issues and Decisions in one controlled place. (Some teams use D for dependencies; Beacon tracks dependencies in the schedule.)

| Type | What it is | Beacon example |
|---|---|---|
| Risk | An uncertain event that would affect objectives if it happened | R-04: the Clinical Information System (CIS) cannot be restored within its 4-hour recovery time objective (RTO) |
| Assumption | Something treated as true without proof | Meridian Clinical Systems (V-01) supports the December restore test |
| Issue | Something happening now that needs action | I-01: Kevin Park (E-009) holds provision, approve and audit-log rights, a segregation-of-duties conflict |
| Decision | A choice made, by whom, when and why | D-01: charter approved by Dr. Helen Marchetti on 2026-09-01 |

Beacon's issues: I-01 the duty conflict; I-02 missed leavers E-014 and E-027 still enabled; I-03 CIS restore tests failed twice. A risk becomes an issue when it happens; an assumption that proves false becomes a risk or an issue. Every entry has an owner, a status and a review date.

read.heading: Writing and assessing a risk
read.body:
Write each risk as cause, event and effect: Because of a cause, an event may happen, which would lead to an effect.

R-04 written this way: Because CIS restore tests took 9.0 and 13.5 hours and the last test was 2025-08-14, the CIS may not be restorable within its 4-hour RTO during an attack, which would leave clinicians on paper for longer than care can safely run. Owner: Daniel Osei (E-004).

Assess each risk for probability and impact, often on a 1 to 5 scale each. Their product gives exposure and a place on a probability-impact matrix, so the highest risks get attention first. Beacon's RAID log rates each as High, Medium or Low, and patient safety and privacy outrank schedule and cost. That is qualitative analysis. Quantitative analysis puts numbers on the overall effect, for example expected monetary value (probability x impact in dollars), and suits the few risks that justify the effort.

| ID | Risk | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| R-01 | Emergency department (ED) extract data quality undermines trust | Tomás Rivera (E-006) |
| R-02 | Small counts at PGH (55 valid visits in Q3) could identify patients | Priya Raman (E-003) |
| R-03 | Multi-factor authentication (MFA) prompts slow clinicians at shared workstations | Janelle Cardinal (E-008) |
| R-05 | Sentinel SOC Services processes security logs in the United States | Priya Raman (E-003) |
| R-06 | Key-person dependency on Tomás Rivera | Programme Manager |
| R-07 | Lumen Analytics Partners' contract ends 2026-11-30 | Programme Manager |
| R-08 | Cost performance could exhaust the management reserve | Marcus Bell (E-002) |

Each also needs a trigger: the early sign that it is about to happen.

read.heading: Choosing risk responses
read.body:
For threats there are five responses:
- Escalate: the risk is outside the programme's authority, so pass it to the right owner.
- Avoid: change the plan to remove the threat.
- Transfer: shift the impact to a third party, usually by contract or insurance. Responsibility for the outcome stays with Kestrel.
- Mitigate: reduce probability or impact.
- Accept: acknowledge it; active acceptance sets aside contingency, passive acceptance does nothing until it happens.

For opportunities: escalate, exploit, share, enhance, accept.

Beacon examples. R-02 is mitigated by Kestrel's rule to suppress counts under 5 outside the care team. R-05 is mitigated: a privacy review, contract safeguards with Sentinel SOC Services and no patient data in the logs, because health information stored or used outside Alberta needs the safeguards the Health Information Act requires (section 60). R-07 is mitigated by knowledge transfer from Lumen before 2026-11-30. R-06 is mitigated by documentation and pairing Mei Tanaka with Tomás Rivera.

After a response, what is left is residual risk; a new risk created by the response is a secondary risk. Both go in the log.

read.heading: Reserves and R-08
read.body:
Contingency reserve funds the responses to identified risks inside the cost baseline. Management reserve, CAD 120,000 held by the sponsor outside the baseline, covers the unforeseen and needs a change decision to release.

At 2026-10-01 the register shows planned value CAD 278,900, earned value CAD 224,000 and actual cost CAD 250,600. The cost performance index (CPI) is 0.89 and the schedule performance index (SPI) 0.80. At a CPI of 0.89 the estimate at completion (EAC) is CAD 1,342,500, a variance at completion of CAD -142,500. Computed: that overrun is CAD 22,500 more than the whole CAD 120,000 reserve, and the EAC is CAD 22,500 above the CAD 1,320,000 total authorized. That is why R-08 exists and why its owner is the Chief Information Officer, Marcus Bell: if the trend holds, Kestrel faces a funding decision, not just a reporting problem. You will work through earned value in full in week 9.

read.heading: Change control
read.body:
Once scope, schedule and cost baselines are approved, they change only through change control. Beacon's process has seven steps, each with an owner and a time target:
1. Raise: the requester completes the change request form; the Programme Manager logs it with an ID (CR-01, CR-02 and so on) within 1 working day.
2. Triage: the Programme Manager checks it and sets the authority level: you alone, the board, or the sponsor.
3. Assess: the data, privacy, security and service leads assess the impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, privacy, security and service support within 5 working days, using the traceability register and the schedule.
4. Decide: the change-control board (CCB), chaired by Marcus Bell (E-002), decides; the sponsor decides anything that moves a gate, uses the reserve or changes a charter objective. The options are approve, approve with conditions, defer or reject, and the reason is recorded.
5. Update baselines: each owner updates and re-versions the affected documents.
6. Implement: a change to a live system also needs an IT change record in the IT Service Management Platform (A-011).
7. Verify and close: the requester confirms the result, the decision is communicated to everyone affected, and the log entry is closed.

Configuration management sits underneath: every document, the semantic model and the reports carry versions, so you always know which baseline is current. An emergency route allows urgent fixes with retrospective review, but it is never a shortcut for wanted features.

In week 7 a request from Janelle Cardinal will test this process. Seniority of the requester never replaces the impact assessment.

read.heading: The CISSP view: risk and change
read.body:
CISSP frames risk as the likelihood that a threat exploits a vulnerability, times the impact on an asset. Management sets risk appetite and accepts residual risk; security professionals advise. At Kestrel, Daniel Osei advises on risk acceptance and the sponsor, Dr. Helen Marchetti, accepts residual risk.

Quantitative terms the exam expects, shown with made-up exam-style numbers, not Kestrel data:
- Single loss expectancy (SLE) = asset value x exposure factor. An asset worth 200,000 with a 25% exposure factor: SLE = 50,000.
- Annualized loss expectancy (ALE) = SLE x annualized rate of occurrence (ARO). If the event is expected once every two years, ARO = 0.5 and ALE = 25,000.
- A control is worth buying if it reduces ALE by more than its yearly cost.

Security change management (Security Operations, 7.9) mirrors the PMP process for live systems: request, security impact review, approval, testing, rollback plan, documentation. Unauthorized change is itself a risk, which is why the CCB also covers changes to the semantic model and row-level security roles.

keyTerms.definition: One controlled log of risks, assumptions, issues and decisions, each with an ID, owner, status and review date.
A risk is uncertain and may happen; an issue is happening now. R-04 is a risk; I-03, the two failed CIS restore tests, is an issue.
The person accountable for monitoring a risk's trigger and carrying out its response, such as Daniel Osei for R-04.
Residual risk remains after a response; secondary risk is a new risk the response creates. Both are logged.
A formal proposal to change a baseline, logged with an ID, assessed for impact and decided by the change-control board.
Single loss expectancy times annualized rate of occurrence: the expected yearly loss from a risk, used to judge whether a control is worth its cost.

build.goal: Open the Beacon RAID log with the canon risks, issues and decision, each owned and assessed, and write the change-control process the board will use for every change to a baseline.
steps: Open Project, Release 1, RAID log. Read How to write it and See the finished example.
Add R-01 to R-08 as cause, event, effect statements with probability and impact (High, Medium or Low), response type and actions, owner, trigger and status.
Add issues I-01, I-02 and I-03 with owner, actions and due date, at least three assumptions (AS-01 onward) with an owner and a check date, and decision D-01 with date, decision maker and effect.
Under R-08, record the computed reserve check: EAC CAD 1,342,500 against total authorized CAD 1,320,000.

Open Change-control process. List the baselines it protects, show the change request form fields, write the seven steps with owners and time targets, and list the impact areas, including privacy and security.

Write the board's terms: chair Marcus Bell, members, the Programme Manager as secretary, quorum, meeting rhythm (every second Thursday and on demand) and decision authority as testable triggers: what you may approve alone, what needs the board, and what needs the sponsor (a gate moves, the reserve is used, a charter objective changes). Then complete Done when and Check yourself for both documents.
build.modelAnswer: A strong RAID log reads cleanly: every risk has a cause, event and effect, a named owner, a trigger and a response type, and issues are kept apart from risks. D-01 carries a date and decision maker. The change-control process names the chair, the impact areas including privacy and security, the decision options and how baselines are updated.

examTips.tip: Business Environment task 5 Plan and manage risk: a risk with a response but no owner is not controlled; assign one. Transfer moves impact, not accountability. Escalate when the risk is outside the project's authority.

Business Environment task 3 Manage and control changes: the first step for any change request, even from an executive, is to log and assess its impact before the board decides. Never implement first and document later.
Security and Risk Management, 1.9 risk management concepts: know SLE = AV x EF and ALE = SLE x ARO, and that senior management, not the security team, accepts residual risk.

Security Operations, 7.9 change management: changes to live systems need request, security impact review, approval, testing, rollback and documentation. An answer that skips testing or rollback is weaker.

pitfalls: Logging issues as risks. I-02, the missed leavers still enabled, is happening now; it needs action today, not a probability score.
Writing risks as single words. 'Data quality' tells nobody what might happen; write the cause, the event and the effect.
Treating transfer as removing the risk. A contract or insurance can shift some financial impact to a third party, but Kestrel stays accountable for the information and the outcome.
Letting seniority bypass change control. A request from a director still gets logged, assessed and decided by the board.

check.q: Is 'the CIS restore tests failed twice' a risk or an issue, and how does it relate to R-04?
check.a: It is an issue (I-03): it has already happened. It is evidence for risk R-04, that the CIS cannot be restored within its 4-hour RTO during a real attack. The issue needs action now, such as finding why restores take 9 to 13.5 hours; the risk needs a response plan and owner.

check.q: Why does R-08 matter if the programme still has a CAD 120,000 management reserve?
check.a: At CPI 0.89 the EAC is CAD 1,342,500, a variance at completion of CAD -142,500. That is CAD 22,500 more than the whole reserve, so if the trend continues Kestrel would exceed its CAD 1,320,000 total authorized funding. The owner, Marcus Bell, must act before the reserve is gone.

check.q: A senior leader asks the analytics team to add a new page to Release 1 directly. What happens under Beacon's change control?
check.a: The request is logged as a change request with an ID, then assessed for impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk, privacy, security and stakeholders. The change-control board chaired by Marcus Bell decides and records why. Only an approved change updates the baselines, and the decision is communicated.
